title: Let no death be in vain
article: Graham Maryancik's sisters have been burning up the phone lines from Alberta since the day he died trying to understand the story as it has so far been told. Police have investigated his death and found that their officer used reasonable force and was justified in his actions.
But the questions persist. Why would Graham attack a police officer? He was trying to leave the lifestyle, was close enough to see the end.
Just days after the court appearance fate made him miss, he was scheduled to take a real estate course and pursue a change in careers.
"He knew he made plenty of mistakes," says his sister Elizabeth. "We were close and we talked about it. He knew he had to get out."
He spoke several times with friends of his on the Lethbridge City police force who counselled and encouraged him.
He confided his plans with his sister and McCabe. This was supposed to be it.
Rhonda Lelek, Graham's mother, says she never would have guessed he would find himself in trouble.
"I never worried about that with him," she says.
"In school he was smart, he was a jock, a popular kid, he was on the football team and girls were after him all the time.
"He had lots of friends, he was always happy and then sometime between 18 and 20 he met some different friends and got involved with drugs.
"But it wasn't the drugs, it was the lure of the money- Up until then I never would have thought he would have done that."
Graham carried the Olympic torch in 1988, played football for the Lethbridge Collegiate Institute Rams and later for the Calgary Dynos.
His family held faith that the birth of his son Cole might bring him back to those days of innocence even if Graham seemed to know different.
"Graham and I once picked the age we would be when we die," says Elizabeth.

"Some people pick how long they think they will live. I never thought my brother would be correct when he said he would be dead before he was 30 years old. He missed his 30th birthday by a few months."
Those answers hopefully await them at a coroner's inquest in Kamloops Sept. 7, 8 and 9.
